skill_traces.query:
Andrew: Hey Audrey! What's up? Missed chatting with ya! Check it out, my girl & I tried out that new cafe scene in the city last weekend! Super fun but kinda sad not being out in nature - that's when I feel like I'm really thriving. Oh man, I miss the peacefulness of being out on a hike.
Audrey: Hey Andrew! That cafe sounds pretty awesome, glad you enjoyed it. Yeah, I know what you mean. That feeling of being out in nature, surrounded by beauty and peace, is unbeatable, compared to being surrounded by concrete jungles. 
Andrew: Yeah, being out in the nature really has a way of taking my breath away. It's like a home for my soul! I feel connected when I'm there.
Audrey: I totally get it. Nature has a way of bringing us back down to earth and reminding us that we're part of something bigger. It's amazing.
Andrew: Yeah, it's like hitting the reset button when life gets too chaotic. Nature has a way of being really soothing.
Audrey: Definitely! For me, taking my dogs for a walk in the park helps me find my center and recharges me. 
Andrew: I hear ya. Can’t do that here unfortunately, city living makes it hard. Really miss that connection and companionship.
Audrey: Must be tough living in the city without the opportunity to go outside. Sure is a different experience.
Andrew: Yeah, it really does. Sometimes it feels like I'm missing out.
Audrey: It must be tough. City life can get overwhelming, so it's great to find ways to connect to nature. What kind of things do you like to do in the city?
Andrew: My girlfriend and I love to discover new places to eat around town. It's a great way to try something new and wind down after a long week.
Audrey: Wow, that sounds like a great way to explore the city! Trying new places and food is always fun. Have you discovered any new favorite spots recently?
Andrew: We found an awesome cafe with amazing pastries - the smell was just irresistible!
Audrey: Sounds amazing! Did you take a photo? I'd love to see!
Andrew: Yep, I got them! Check out this photo of the delicious pastries we had at the cafe.
Audrey: Wow, they look great! What did you get? Now I'm craving pastries!
Andrew: They taste great too! We had some delicious croissants, muffins, and tarts! It was amazing!
Audrey: Wow, sounds amazing! Glad you got to enjoy them. Since you metioned pastries, I made some of my favorite treats last week. Let's have a pastry party sometime! 
Andrew: That looks delicious! A pastry party sounds awesome, count me in!
Audrey: Awesome! My dogs will tag along. My furry friends would love it!
Andrew: Definitely! They'll have a great time at the party! Can't wait for the party!
Audrey: Same! Looking forward to it. This would be a good chance for you to hang out with them.
Andrew: Yeah! It's gonna be awesome to see all of them together and chowing down. Super excited!
Audrey: Yay! This'll be awesome! Seeing them all together, having fun and enjoying treats is the best. I can't imagine life without them, they bring so much joy.
Andrew: Aww, so cute! I bet their happy faces means a lot to you.
Audrey: I know right? They mean the world to me. So much that I got tattoos of them on my arm.
Andrew: Wow, that tattoo looks great!
Audrey: Thanks! I got it a while ago. It represents my love for my pups and nature's beauty.
Andrew: Aww, that's cute! What made you getting the tattoo?
Audrey: I've always had a strong bond with them – they make me so happy, and I just want to see their happy faceseven when thry're not with me.
Andrew: That's awesome, I'm glad they bring so much joy into your life.

selected.name: Extract Comfort and Joy Sources
selected.description: Use when a message states that something cheers the user up, brings joy, or provides comfort.
content: During extraction, if the user mentions a pet, hobby, person, item, or activity that provides cheer, comfort, or emotional support, create a separate durable memory (preference, relationship, or state) capturing that source, even when the message also contains stress or negative events.
Do not merge the supportive source only into a negative-event candidate; it should be its own candidate so it survives later SKIP/MERGE decisions.
Extract only sources explicitly stated as supportive; do not infer unmentioned ones.

selected.name: Extract Photo-Sharing Events
selected.description: When a message presents an object or result with visual language like 'Here are...' or explicitly mentions sharing a photo, during extraction.
content: When a message uses presentation phrasing such as 'Here are...', 'Check out...', 'This is a photo of...', or 'Attached is...' to introduce something, record that the speaker shared a photo of that item, even if the word 'photo' does not appear.

If the speaker explicitly mentions sharing, sending, or showing a picture/photo/image, create an event memory that records the sharing action and the described content (e.g., subject or creator of the picture).
Preserve the literal object named in the message (e.g., picture) — do not replace it with an inferred object such as a bookshelf, item, or possession.
Keep the sharing act within the same event memory as the other facts from that message; do not summarize away the visual sharing.
Only include facts explicitly stated; do not convert a shared picture into an ownership claim unless ownership is directly stated.
selected.rerank_reason: Andrew shares a photo of pastries, which directly involves the act of sharing a photo and fits the skill's criteria for extracting photo-sharing events.

nearby_not_selected.name: Location Qualifiers for Named Destination Plans
nearby_not_selected.description: When extracting or updating a plan memory that mentions a specific named venue, landmark, or business, include its commonly known location(s) so future location questions can be answered.
content: During extraction, if a plan memory mentions a specific named venue, landmark, or business, add a concise qualifier naming its well-known location(s), e.g., US states or countries.
Use only common knowledge about that entity; do not research or speculate beyond obvious, widely known locations.
If one location is commonly known, record it; if several prominent locations exist, record all commonly known ones, then stop.
Apply the same qualifier when updating an existing plan memory that references the venue.

nearby_not_selected.name: Extract Concrete Activity from Follow-Up Clarification
nearby_not_selected.description: Use when a message describes an activity vaguely and the next message names the concrete result.
content: During extraction, treat any message reporting the speaker performing an activity as a candidate source, even when the object is only a photo or pronoun.
If the following message from another participant identifies the concrete object or result, extract an event memory capturing who did what, using both messages as evidence.
Do not skip follow-up messages that clarify or name an earlier activity.

nearby_not_selected.name: Extract Statements of Personal Significance
nearby_not_selected.description: Use when a user says an object, photo, or item reminds them of someone or something, or has personal meaning.
content: During extraction, when a user describes an object, photo, or item as reminding them of someone or something ('reminds me of', 'makes me think of', 'means ... to me'), create a candidate state memory capturing the connection.
Record who is reminded (the speaker), the object, and what it reminds them of (person, feeling, or value) in the speaker's own words.
Treat such statements as durable personal facts even though they are phrased as effects or feelings, not as direct assertions; extract at most one memory per statement.

nearby_not_selected.name: Extract Origin Events as Distinct Memories
nearby_not_selected.description: When a user explains how they started or got into an activity, hobby, or interest, including who introduced it or when it began.
content: During extraction, if a message contains an origin narrative (how the person started an activity, who introduced it, what prompted it, or a concrete start time), create a separate event memory for the origin in addition to any preference or state memory.
Record the causal source (person or circumstance) and the start time/age if stated; do not fold the origin into a generic preference summary.
If the origin names another person, also consider a relationship memory capturing that connection.
Emit at most one origin memory per activity per message; skip if the same origin is repeated later.

nearby_not_selected.name: Capture likely deceased from euphemistic absence language
nearby_not_selected.description: During extraction, when a speaker describes someone with euphemistic absence language (e.g., 'will never be able to...', 'I miss him/her here') that strongly implies death, use this guidance.
content: When a statement euphemistically implies a person has died without explicitly saying so, also extract the implied state that the person is likely deceased, in addition to the literal statement.
Record the inference with an appropriate hedge (e.g., 'likely deceased') because the speaker did not state it directly; do not assert cause, date, or circumstances of death.
Stop after capturing the likely-deceased state and the literal content; do not extrapolate further details about the person or the relationship.
